blocks.text: Dragons differ from serpents chiefly in bulk. Accordingly, as we said, the dragon is defined in Alcamus as حية عظيمة [ḥayya ʿaẓīma], a great serpent. And well known is the proverb of the Greeks, Ὄφις, εἰ μὴ φάγῃ ὄφιν, δράκων οὐ γενήσεται [Ophis, ei mē phagē ophin, drakōn ou genēsetai]· A serpent, unless it has eaten a serpent, will not become a dragon. Nor without reason does Augustine say on Psalm. CXLVIII.: Dragons are certain great animals; there are none greater upon the earth. But no one could easily say how large they grow, since here the ancients tell many fables, and nowhere is there greater licence for lying, as we shall now show step by step. Pliny, book 8, ch. 13, reports from Juba that among the Asachaean Ethiopians crested dragons of twenty cubits are bred. Aëtius and Avicenna write that they grow from five cubits up to thirty. This is confirmed from elsewhere too. For in Aelian, History book 2, chapter 21, dragons in Phrygia grow to ten orgyiae; and that each of these is three cubits, Hesychius and Eustathius teach. And Pausanias in the Corinthiaca relates that τοὺς ὄφεις τοὺς Μεγαλαύνας [tous opheis tous Megalaunas], the Megalaunian serpents around Epidaurus grow beyond a size of thirty cubits; such as are said to be bred in India and in Africa. So Philostratus, book 3, ch. 2, where he treats of the species of dragons in India: Οἱ μὲν δὴ ἕλειοι νωθροί τέ εἰσι, καὶ τριακοντάπηχυ μῆκος ἔχουσι [Hoi men dē heleioi nōthroi te eisi, kai triakontapēchy mēkos echousi]· The marsh ones are sluggish, and thirty cubits long. The same was the measure of the Egyptian dragon that was brought alive to Alexandria to Ptolemy Philadelphus. For Tzetzes is mistaken, who makes it τριακονταπεντάπηχυν [triakontapentapēchyn], of thirty-five cubits, Chiliad 3, History 113, since the author he follows, Diodorus, book 3, asserts in express words that it was only τριάκοντα πηχῶν [triakonta pēchōn], of thirty cubits. That he saw one such, Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 41, testifies in these words: Τῶν μέν τοι ὑπὸ τὴν ἡμετέραν ὄψιν πεπτωκότων ὁ μέγιστος, πέφηνε πηχῶν τριάκοντα [Tōn men toi hypo tēn hēmeteran opsin peptōkotōn ho megistos, pephēne pēchōn triakonta]· The largest of those that came under our eyes appeared to be thirty cubits. And in Strabo, book 16: δρακόντων εἴρηκε μεγέθη τριάκοντα πηχῶν ὁ Ἀρτεμίδωρος, ἐλέφαντας καὶ ταύρους χειρουμένων [drakontōn eirēke megethē triakonta pēchōn ho Artemidōros, elephantas kai taurous cheiroumenōn], Artemidorus describes dragons of thirty cubits, which overpower bulls and elephants. I am willing, therefore, that what so many of the ancients attest be held true: that dragons in the bulk of their body reach a measure of thirty cubits [col. 431] or, what is the same, forty-five feet. But most of what follows surpasses belief. In the Periplus of the Red Sea, in Aelian, book 17, ch. 1, Alexander reports that he saw serpents forty cubits in length, to which their breadth and thickness corresponded in proportion. [III, 226] Philostorgius, book 3, ch. 11, mentions dragons in the East and the South, πάχος μὲν δοκῶν οὐκ ἐλάττους, τὸ δὲ μῆκος εἰς δέκα πέντε παρατεινόμενον ὀργυίας [pachos men dokōn ouk elattous, to de mēkos eis deka pente parateinomenon orgyias], not smaller than beams in thickness, and extending in length to fifteen orgyiae (that is, 45 cubits), whose skins, brought to Rome, he himself saw. Suetonius, ch. 43, relates that Augustus exhibited a snake of fifty cubits before the comitium. And under the same emperor Dio, book 50, mentions Τοῦ δικεφάλου δράκοντος τοῦ ἐν τῇ Τυρσηνίδι φανέντος, καὶ ἐς πέντε καὶ ὀγδοήκοντα πόδας ἐξικνουμένου, πολλά τε κακώσαντος, εἶτα κεραυνωθέντος [Tou dikephalou drakontos tou en tē Tyrsēnidi phanentos, kai es pente kai ogdoēkonta podas exikneoumenou, polla te kakōsantos, eita keraunōthentos], a two-headed dragon seen in Etruria, eighty-five feet long, which, after it had laid waste much, was struck by lightning. Of the same kind is what Posidonius in Strabo, book 16, relates of the plain of Coele-Syria, Macra: τὸν δράκοντα πεπτωκότα ὁραθῆναι νεκρὸν, μῆκος σχεδόν τι καὶ πλεθριαῖον, πάχος δ᾽, ὥς θ᾽ ἱππέας ἑκατέρωθεν παραστάντας ἀλλήλους μὴ καθορᾷν, χάσμα δὲ ὥς τ᾽ ἔφιππον δέξασθαι, τῆς δὲ φολίδος λεπίδα ἑκάστην ὑπεραίρουσαν θυρεοῦ [ton drakonta peptōkota horathēnai nekron, mēkos schedon ti kai plethriaion, pachos d᾽, hōs th᾽ hippeas hekaterōthen parastantas allēlous mē kathoran, chasma de hōs t᾽ ephippon dexasthai, tēs de pholidos lepida hekastēn hyperairousan thyreou], that a dead dragon was seen, a plethrum (or a hundred feet) in length, and of such thickness that horsemen standing on either side could not see one another; and with a gaping mouth so wide that it could take in a man sitting on a horse; and finally, each scale of whose skin was larger than a shield. Now what is better known than the dragon of one hundred and twenty feet which Regulus is said to have found lurking by the river Bagradas, not far from Utica? When it was attacked in vain with missiles and javelins by the whole army, it was at last overcome with ballistae and siege engines, like some town. And its skin and jaws lasted in a temple at Rome until the Numantine war. Many writers attest this. But see especially Tubero in Gellius, book 6, ch. 3, Livy in Valerius, book 1, at the end, Pliny, book 8, ch. 14, and Orosius, book 4, ch. 8. What of the fact that Ethiopian and Indian dragons are read not only to equal so portentous a bulk but even to surpass it? For to the Ethiopian ones Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 21, ^{(2)}, assigns a length of thirty orgyiae, that is, ninety cubits, or 135 feet. And in the same country there were those who openly asserted that they had seen dragons a hundred cubits long, that is, a hundred and fifty feet; but that their credit is suspect, Diodorus, book 3, testifies in these words: Those who inhabit the region (of Ethiopia) near the desert and full of wild beasts say that many kinds of serpents, incredible in size, are seen. Ἑκατὸν γὰρ πηχῶν τὸ μῆκος ἑωρακέναι τινὲς ἀποφαινόμενοι, δικαίως ἂν οὐχ᾽ ὑφ᾽ ἡμῶν μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν ἄλλων ἁπάντων ψευδολογεῖν ὑπολεφθείησαν [Hekaton gar pēchōn to mēkos heōrakenai tines apophainomenoi, dikaiōs an ouch᾽ hyph᾽ hēmōn monon, alla kai hypo tōn allōn hapantōn pseudologein hypolephtheiēsan], for some, declaring that they have seen them a hundred cubits long, are justly suspected of lying, not only by us but by all others too. As for the Indian ones, Aelian, [III, 227] book 15, ch. 21, mentions one seventy cubits long, or a hundred and five feet, with eyes like a Macedonian shield, worshipped by the Indians with the greatest reverence in a certain cave, which by its breath and hissing alone terrified and threw into confusion the whole army of Alexander. But, as if this were too little, in the same author, book 16, ch. 39, Onesicritus relates that Aposisares the Indian kept two dragons, of which the smaller was eighty cubits, that is, a hundred and twenty feet, the larger a hundred and forty cubits, that is, two hundred and ten feet, which Alexander greatly desired to see. The same you may read in Tzetzes, Chiliad 3, History 113. But Strabo, who writes Biasarus or Abiosarus instead of Aposisares, thus undermines the credit of this fiction: Ἐν τοῖς ὄρεσιν ἡ τοῦ Βιασάρου (MSS. Ἀβιοσάρου) χώρα, παρ᾽ ᾧ δύο δράκοντας ἀπήγγελον οἱ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ πρέσβεις τρέφεσθαι, [col. 432] τὸν μὲν ὀγδοήκοντα πηχῶν, τὸν δὲ τετταράκοντα πρὸς τοῖς ἑκατὸν, ὡς εἴρηκεν Ὀνησίκριτος, ὃν ἐκ Ἀλεξάνδρου μᾶλλον ἢ τῶν παραδόξων Ἀλεξάνδρου ἀρχικυβερνήτην προσείποι τις ἄν [En tois oresin hē tou Biasarou (MSS. Abiosarou) chōra, par᾽ hō dyo drakontas apēngelon hoi par᾽ autou presbeis trephesthai, ton men ogdoēkonta pēchōn, ton de tettarakonta pros tois hekaton, hōs eirēken Onēsikritos, hon ek Alexandrou mallon ē tōn paradoxōn Alexandrou archikybernētēn prosei pois an]· In the mountains is the country of Biasarus (or Abiosarus), with whom, as the envoys sent by him reported, two dragons were kept, one of eighty, the other of a hundred and forty cubits, on the authority of Onesicritus, whom one might justly call the chief pilot not so much of Alexander's ship as of incredible tales. Yet this is not yet the end of the lies. For these may seem trifles compared with the report that Taxiles, a king neighbouring Abiosarus, showed Alexander a dragon of five plethra, that is, five hundred feet. So Maximus of Tyre, Oration 38: Ἔδειξε καὶ ζῶον ὑπερφυὲς, Διονύσου ἄγαλμα, ᾧ Ἰνδοὶ ἔθυον, δράκων ἦν μῆκος πεντάπλεθρον [Edeixe kai zōon hyperphyes, Dionysou agalma, hō Indoi ethyon, drakōn ēn mēkos pentaplethron], He showed a certain immense animal, an image of Bacchus, to which the Indians sacrificed, namely a dragon five plethra in length. Meanwhile the Greeks are far more modest than the Arabs, one of whom, in Damiri, asserts that he saw تنينا طوله نحو فرسخين ولونه مثل لون النمر مفلسا مثل فلوس السمك بجناحين عظيمين علي هية جناح السمك وراسها كراس الانسان لكنها كالتل العظيم [tinnīnan ṭūluhu naḥwa farsakhayn wa-lawnuhu mithl lawn al-namir mufallasan mithl fulūs al-samak bi-janāḥayn ʿaẓīmayn ʿalī hya janāḥ al-samak wa-rāsuhā ka-rās al-insān lākinnahā kal-tall al-ʿaẓīm] a dragon nearly two parasangs long (that is, eight thousand paces), of the colour of a leopard, scaled with the scales of a fish, furnished also with great fins, like fishes, and having a human head the size of a lofty hill.
